title: The British-Spelling Nationality Head
takeaway: A single attention head is read two ways at once: by its attention pattern on a passage, and by pushing each of its four weight matrices through the J-lens. The two readings agree — the head fires on British spellings and writes Commonwealth nationality — which is the paper's demonstration that composing the lens with a component's weights can name what that component reads and what it writes, using no prompt data at all.
walkthrough:
### What the item is

The article renders this as a live widget rather than a fixed image, so the exact controls are not pinned down by the text. It has two halves. One half is a passage of text with an [[attention-head]]'s attention pattern drawn over it. The other half is four short lists of vocabulary tokens, one list per weight matrix of that same head.

### Reading the attention half

Certain tokens in the passage are drawn with a box around them. A boxed token is a query position — the position the head attends *from*. The widget displays the attention from each boxed token back over the earlier tokens.

The paper reports the same shape for every box. Each boxed token is a British spelling: centre, labour, colour, behaviour, honour. Each attends back to a nearby Commonwealth country word: African, Zealand, Australian, British, Canadian.

### Reading the four token lists

A head has four weight matrices — query, key, value and output. Query, key and value read from the [[residual-stream]]; output writes back into it.

Each matrix is composed with the [[jacobian-lens]] map $W_U J$, whose rows are the [[j-lens-vector]]s, one per vocabulary token. That composition, written $W_U\,J\,W_{\{Q,K,V,O\}}$ in the caption, again gives one row per token. Tokens are then ranked by the norm of their row.

A large norm means that token's lens direction is one the matrix picks up strongly, whether reading or writing. No prompt enters this calculation; it runs on the weights alone, which is the point of [[component-interpretation]].

### What the lists say

The query side reads colour, centre, neighbour and other British spellings. The key side reads a mixture of British spellings and country names. The value and output sides read Australian, Australia, Canadian and related tokens.

So the input side of the head is spelling and the output side is nationality. The paper's reading follows: the head detects a British-spelled word at the current position, attends to a Commonwealth country mentioned nearby, and writes that country's representation into the residual stream.

A use for this is offered only speculatively — spelling might help the model settle whose nationality is in play when a context names several speakers.

One caveat sits in the next paragraph of the paper. Of the three further heads shown after this one, it notes that many heads with interpretable projections have similar vocabulary rankings across all four matrices. The input-versus-output contrast here is therefore weaker evidence than it first looks.

terms.definition: The caption's name for what the head does: it takes a British-spelled word as its trigger and produces a Commonwealth country's representation as its output. The arrow denotes an input-to-output transformation, not an arithmetic operation.
The transformer operation that lets one token position retrieve and transform information from earlier positions. Here a single head is the object under study.
The distribution, for a given query position, of how much weight the head places on each earlier position. It is drawn over the passage in one half of the widget.
A token in the passage drawn with a box around it, marking it as one of the query positions whose attention the widget displays. Every boxed token in this figure is a British spelling.
The position the head attends from — the token whose residual stream is projected through the query matrix to decide where to look. In this figure these are the boxed British spellings.

The British-spelled words named in the text as boxed query tokens. Each differs from its American spelling (center, labor, color, behavior, honor), which is what makes the spelling itself informative about a writer.

A further British spelling that appears in the query-side lens readout but is not listed among the boxed tokens. Its presence indicates the query matrix reads the British-spelling family broadly, not only the words present in this passage.

The tokens the boxed positions attend back to. They are fragments of Commonwealth country and nationality names — South African, New Zealand, and so on — rather than whole words, because the tokenizer splits them.
The tokens named as topping the value-side and output-side lens readouts. They are what the head writes into the residual stream, as opposed to what it looks for.

The grouping of countries — Australia, Canada, New Zealand, South Africa, the United Kingdom — that share British spelling conventions. The head's output tokens fall inside this set, which is why the caption uses the word.

The paper's technique: a per-layer averaged Jacobian $J$ that, composed with the unembedding, turns any residual-stream direction into a ranked list of vocabulary tokens the direction disposes the model to say.
One row of $W_U J$: the residual-stream direction associated with a single vocabulary token. This figure ranks these vectors by how strongly each of the head's matrices engages them.
The unembedding matrix, the model's own final linear map from the residual stream to a score per vocabulary token. It is what turns a direction into words.

The averaged Jacobian at the head's layer, mapping a perturbation of the residual stream there to its first-order effect on the final-layer residual stream, averaged over positions and over a corpus of prompts.

The head's query projection, which reads the current position's residual stream to form the vector that decides where to attend. Its lens readout says which token concepts trigger the head at the current position.
The head's key projection, which reads each earlier position to form the vector matched against the query. Its lens readout says which token concepts make an earlier position a candidate target.
The head's value projection, which reads the content the head will carry from the attended position. Its lens readout says what the head picks up once it has decided where to look.
The head's output projection, which writes the attended content back into the residual stream. Its lens readout says what the head deposits for later layers to use.

The caption's compact notation for the four compositions, one per weight matrix, of the lens map with that matrix. The brace set is shorthand for running the same calculation four times, once with each of Q, K, V and O.

The length of a token's row in the composed matrix, used here as the ranking score. A long row means the head's matrix engages that token's lens direction strongly; the sign and direction within the head's subspace are discarded.
The head of the ranked list — the vocabulary entries with the largest composed-row norms. The paper reads a component's function off these, and only when the ranking is sharply peaked.
The running per-position vector that every layer reads from and writes to. Query, key and value read from it; output writes back into it; and the lens is defined over directions in it.
The value-and-output pair taken together — what the head writes about whatever it attended to, independent of where it attended. In this head, that content is Commonwealth nationality.

numbers.meaning: The figure's number in the article. It sits in appendix section 10.24.3, among the examples of interpreting model components with the J-lens.
The number of weight matrices an attention head has — query, key, value and output — and therefore the number of token lists shown. The count is fixed by the architecture, not chosen by the authors.
The number of British-spelled query tokens the surrounding text names: centre, labour, colour, behaviour, honour. The widget itself may box more; five is what the prose enumerates.
The number of attended Commonwealth tokens the text names: African, Zealand, Australian, British, Canadian. Again this is the prose's enumeration rather than a stated total.
The number of query-side lens tokens quoted — colour, centre, neighbour — before the text falls back on "and other British spellings". The list is truncated in the prose, not in the widget.
The number of value- and output-side lens tokens quoted: Australian, Australia, Canadian. The text adds "and related tokens" rather than giving a full list.

No attention weights, norms, ranks or layer index are reported for this head anywhere in the caption or the surrounding text. The evidence is presented as a qualitative token ordering, which is why the paper says the readouts "suggest" the head's function rather than measuring it.
